describe.readme:
# Heilbronn triangles

Place 11 points inside a triangle. Make the smallest triangle formed by any three points as large as possible. Your submission is a set of coordinates.

## Run the starter

The starter in `examples/baseline/` scores about **0.0317227922** at the default
settings. That means its smallest triangle occupies about **3.17%** of the
container's area. Higher is better, and the same coordinates give the same score.

**On AutoLab:** Click **Start a climb**, then **Climb on AutoLab**. Choose an agent
model and either a connected CPU machine or **CPU only (small)**. Set a model
budget under **More options**. AutoLab copies the starter into your climb. Read
its baseline result before reviewing the agent's changes; pause when you want
to stop.

**Locally:** Choose **Climb locally** and paste its setup prompt into your coding
agent. Ask it to run the starter first. Once the hill is downloaded, run these
commands from the project folder containing `.autolab/`:

```sh
cp -R .autolab/hills/heilbronn-triangle/examples/baseline ./my-points
hills eval ./my-points -H heilbronn-triangle -o baseline.json
```

Use a fresh `my-points` folder. The report should say `passed: true` and show
`min_area` near **0.0317227922**. The evaluator needs Python 3.11 or newer;
its environment installs `mpmath` automatically. No GPU or private dataset is
required. Local results are not automatically added to AutoLab's leaderboard.

## Compute and cost

The agent model writes experiments; the compute runs them. The model budget covers model calls. Rented compute is billed separately. Pause the climb to stop experiments and release AutoLab rentals; your own connected machine remains yours to manage.

Before changing anything, open the baseline job and check for a passing score. **Nodes offline** means compute is disconnected, not that your solution failed.

## Try a first change

On AutoLab, ask the agent to make this edit, then run one evaluation. For local work, edit your copied submission folder.

Open `my-points/points.json`. Each pair is a point's `[x, y]` coordinate.
Try changing the first point's x coordinate from `"0.335538289274"` to
`"0.335638289274"`, leaving its y coordinate and all other points unchanged:

```sh
hills eval ./my-points -H heilbronn-triangle -o attempt-1.json
```

Compare the score and `details.smallest_triangle` in the two reports. Those
three indices identify the points currently limiting the score; counting starts
at zero. A valid edit can improve the score, lower it, or leave it unchanged if
a different triangle is the limiting one. Keep a copy of the starter so you can
undo an edit.

Once that makes sense, try small perturbations of individual points, keeping
valid improvements. You may write a search program, but keep the hill's
evaluator unchanged. The submission is the `points.json` your program produces.

## What to submit

Submit a directory containing `points.json`, a JSON array of exactly 11 pairs
`[x, y]`. The container has corners `(0, 0)`, `(1, 0)` and `(0.5, sqrt(3)/2)`.
Points may lie on the boundary. Two coinciding points or three collinear points
make the minimum area zero and are rejected.

You may change every coordinate and use any method to find an arrangement.
Coordinates can be JSON numbers or numeric strings such as `"0.288675134594813"`.
Strings preserve the supplied decimal digits. There is a limit of 200 significant
digits per coordinate; a nonzero coordinate cannot have magnitude below `1e-60`.

## Read the result

**`min_area` is the smallest triangle's area divided by the container's area.**
The evaluator computes it from all triples of points. The details include
`min_area_30_digits` and `smallest_triangle` for a closer look at the result.

A failed result explains the problem in `details.error`, such as a point outside
the container, the wrong number of points, or collinear points. Correct that
problem before comparing scores.

## Reference construction

`examples/alphaevolve/` contains a stronger reference arrangement, scoring about
**0.0365298899** here. The [2025 AlphaEvolve paper, section B.9](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/DeepMind.com/Blog/alphaevolve-a-gemini-powered-coding-agent-for-designing-advanced-algorithms/AlphaEvolve.pdf)
reported a construction above 0.0365, improving on the earlier 0.036 result.
These are dated reference values, not a claim about the current record. Running
the supplied arrangement reproduces that example; copying it is not a new discovery.

## Precision and other settings

Triangle determinants are computed with exact rational arithmetic. The final
division by the container area uses 60-digit arithmetic because it involves
`sqrt(3)`. Containment allows `1e-12` of slack for coordinates rounded near an
edge; the area uses the coordinates as submitted.

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `n` | 11 | Required point count; different counts compare separately |

To try another point count, supply a matching array and use, for example,
`hills eval ./my-points -H heilbronn-triangle -p n=12`.

There is no held-out data. `--final` performs the same computation and records a
separate test-mode report. Keep reports unedited; `hills verify` checks their
signatures using the matching signing key.

## If the first run fails

- **Wrong point count:** submit exactly 11 pairs in `points.json`.
- **Outside the triangle:** check the point index reported in `details.error`.
- **Zero-area triangle:** two points coincide or three are collinear. Restore the starter, then try a smaller edit.

Use `details.smallest_triangle` to find the three points limiting a valid result. Compare `min_area` at the same point count; higher is better.

## Versions and comparisons

A climb stays on the hill version selected when it was created. To try a newly published version, start a new climb from the hill page. Old results stay with their original version, including when a new version only changes this README.
